key_points: Conservative treatment (counselling, exercises, occlusal splint therapy, massage, manual therapy) should be the first-line approach for TMD pain due to low risk of side effects.
Laser therapy at 904 nm and 700 Hz is mentioned as a method for treating inflammatory processes in TMD, with reported penetration depth of 30 mm.

Pharmacotherapy for TMD includes NSAIDs (ibuprofen 400–800 mg/day, meloxicam 7.5–15 mg/day, diclofenac 50 mg TID, naproxen sodium 500 mg BID), acetaminophen (325–1000 mg/day), muscle relaxants, benzodiazepines, tricyclic antidepressants, and corticosteroids.
Botulinum toxin type A (BTX-A) is supported by clinical investigations for disc displacement and bruxism-related myofascial pain.
Doxycycline and other tetracyclines can help prevent condylar resorption by inhibiting matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs).
Arthrocentesis reduces pain and functional impairment more rapidly than conservative treatment, but long-term outcomes are comparable.
Intra-articular injections of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) are described as a valid procedure for decreasing TMD pain.
Acupuncture is reported to be effective in long-term follow-ups (18–20 years) for TMD pain management.
In rheumatoid disorders with TMJ involvement, systemic methotrexate and/or TNF inhibitors are the primary pharmacologic treatment.
Benzodiazepines (diazepam 5 mg, lorazepam 1 mg, alprazolam 0.5 mg) for 5–10 days are recommended for anxiety and stress relief in TMD.

outcomes.measured: Effectiveness of conservative treatment vs. arthrocentesis for TMD pain
outcomes.result: Arthrocentesis reduces pain and functional impairment more rapidly; long-term outcomes comparable between both modalities
outcomes.clinical_significance: Arthrocentesis may be preferred for faster relief but conservative treatment achieves similar long-term results

outcomes.measured: Muscular therapy effectiveness in TMD patients
outcomes.clinical_significance: Less effective in patients with limited mouth opening due to muscular or joint pain

outcomes.measured: Occlusal splint therapy (SVED appliance) effect on TMD symptoms
outcomes.result: Decreases head and spine aches and disc displacements within 3 weeks; further improvement at 3 months
outcomes.clinical_significance: Clinically meaningful reduction in symptoms and unblocking of limited mouth opening

notes: This narrative review covers the full spectrum of TMD treatment modalities. Laser therapy is mentioned briefly (904 nm, 700 Hz, 30 mm depth) without detailed clinical protocol parameters. Multiple drug classes are discussed with specific dosing recommendations. The paper was published in The Journal of Headache and Pain (2015).

contraindications: Massage pressure that is too intense may lead to increased muscular tonus — pressure must be gradual and moderate.
Cryotherapy carries a high risk of frostbite; cold compresses should not exceed 10–15 minutes.
NSAIDs carry risk of hypertension exacerbation and gastrointestinal ulcerations.
COX-2-selective NSAIDs (celecoxib, meloxicam) are not found to be superior for TMD treatment despite fewer side effects.
Pharmacotherapy alone is considered only palliative for TMD; exceptions are systemic diseases with TMJ involvement.
adverse_events: NSAIDs: gastrointestinal upset, ulcerations, hypertension exacerbation.
Cryotherapy: frostbite risk with prolonged application.
Benzodiazepines: CNS effects; recommended only for short-term use (5–10 days).
Muscle relaxants, opiates, anticonvulsants, ketamine, TCAs: no evidence for efficacy in TMD; risk of systemic side effects.

drugs_mentioned.name: acetaminophen
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: First medication of choice for moderate TMD pain relief; average daily dose 325–1000 mg.

drugs_mentioned.name: ibuprofen
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: High efficiency for TMD pain relief; average daily dose 400–800 mg. Risk of GI upset and hypertension.

drugs_mentioned.name: meloxicam
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Used for TMD pain; average daily dose 7.5–15 mg. Fewer GI side effects than non-selective NSAIDs but not proven superior for TMD.

drugs_mentioned.name: diclofenac
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Used for arthritis-related TMD pain; maximum dose 50 mg orally 3 times daily.

drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Used for arthritis-related TMD pain; 500 mg twice daily.

drugs_mentioned.name: celecoxib
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: COX-2-selective NSAID with fewer GI side effects; not found superior for TMD treatment.

drugs_mentioned.name: baclofen
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Used clinically for TMJ management; no evidence for efficacy in TMD.

drugs_mentioned.name: tizanidine
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Used clinically for TMJ management; no evidence for efficacy in TMD.

drugs_mentioned.name: cyclobenzaprine
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Used clinically for TMJ management; no evidence for efficacy in TMD.

drugs_mentioned.name: metaxolone
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Recommended for myorelaxation with low CNS impact; average daily dose 800 mg.

drugs_mentioned.name: morphine
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Used clinically for TMJ management; no evidence for efficacy in TMD.

drugs_mentioned.name: gabapentin
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Used clinically for TMJ management; no evidence for efficacy in TMD.

drugs_mentioned.name: ketamine
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Used clinically for TMJ management; no evidence for efficacy in TMD.

drugs_mentioned.name: amitriptyline
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Used for chronic TMD pain and neuropathic pain; manages headaches and improves sleep quality. No evidence for efficacy specifically in TMD.
drugs_mentioned.laser_implication: Tricyclic antidepressants may increase photosensitivity; consider when planning laser/light therapy in TMD patients on amitriptyline.

drugs_mentioned.name: lidocaine
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: 1 ml of 2% lidocaine without vasoconstrictor used for analgesic blockage in acute muscle spasms to allow therapeutic stretching.

drugs_mentioned.name: dipyrone
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: 500 mg 3 times daily for 2 days as complementary therapy in acute muscle spasms; may be combined with orfendrine (muscle relaxant).

drugs_mentioned.name: diazepam
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: 5 mg for 5–10 days for anxiety and stress relief in TMD; short-term use only.

drugs_mentioned.name: lorazepam
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: 1 mg for 5–10 days for anxiety and stress relief in TMD; short-term use only.

drugs_mentioned.name: alprazolam
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: 0.5 mg for 5–10 days for anxiety and stress relief in TMD; short-term use only.

drugs_mentioned.name: botulinum toxin type A
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Injected into lateral pterygoid muscles for disc displacement; reduces myofascial pain and bruxism symptoms. Used for bruxism, oromandibular dystonia, trismus, masseter/temporalis hypertrophy, headaches.

drugs_mentioned.name: hyaluronic acid
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Intra-articular injection for TMJ inflammatory disorders as anti-inflammatory agent.

drugs_mentioned.name: corticosteroids
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Single intramuscular dose for myositis and inflammatory disorders; intra-articular injection for TMJ. Also used systemically in JIA/RA with TMJ involvement.

drugs_mentioned.name: doxycycline
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Helps prevent condylar resorption by inhibiting matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs); medication of choice in patients undergoing orthognathic surgery.
drugs_mentioned.laser_implication: Doxycycline is a known photosensitizer; patients on doxycycline undergoing laser therapy in the orofacial region should be monitored for photosensitivity reactions.

drugs_mentioned.name: methotrexate
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Systemic treatment for JIA/RA with TMJ involvement; primary pharmacologic treatment in rheumatoid TMD.
drugs_mentioned.laser_implication: Methotrexate may increase photosensitivity; relevant consideration for laser/light therapy in patients with rheumatoid TMD.

drugs_mentioned.name: TNF inhibitors
drugs_mentioned.dental_relevance: Used in JIA/RA with TMJ involvement; primary pharmacologic treatment in rheumatoid TMD. Immunosuppressive effects relevant to dental procedures.

perioperative_consideration: Patients with TMD on doxycycline or methotrexate may have increased photosensitivity relevant to laser/light therapy. Patients on benzodiazepines or muscle relaxants may have altered sedation response. NSAIDs increase bleeding risk perioperatively. Patients on TNF inhibitors or methotrexate are immunosuppressed — increased infection risk with invasive procedures. Botulinum toxin injections require careful anatomical knowledge of masticatory muscles.
uncertainties: Laser therapy parameters (904 nm, 700 Hz) are mentioned only briefly without power, fluence, spot size, application time, or number of sessions — no complete clinical protocol extractable.
The paper does not specify which laser device or brand is used for the 904 nm / 700 Hz protocol.
Photosensitivity classification for amitriptyline is based on general pharmacological knowledge, not explicitly stated in this paper.
Photosensitivity classification for methotrexate is based on general pharmacological knowledge, not explicitly stated in this paper.

critical_notes: ⚠️ Este protocolo es de carácter teórico/revisión. Los parámetros clínicos completos (potencia, fluencia, tiempo de aplicación, número de sesiones) no están especificados en el paper original.
El paper menciona únicamente longitud de onda (904 nm) y frecuencia (700 Hz) con profundidad de penetración de 30 mm; no se reportan otros parámetros técnicos.
El documento presenta esta técnica como un método que 'ha ganado popularidad' para procesos inflamatorios en TMD, sin proporcionar evidencia clínica propia ni protocolo detallado.
El documento presenta esta técnica favorablemente; existen alternativas con mecanismos de acción diferentes (diodo 810–980 nm, Er:YAG, Nd:YAG) que pueden ser apropiadas según el caso clínico.

protocols.evidence_level: Bajo — revisión narrativa. El paper menciona el láser 904 nm como método con popularidad creciente pero no aporta datos de RCTs ni parámetros clínicos estandarizados. Basado en: Wieckiewicz et al. 2015.
